title: Knife skills
learner_summary: A home cook who has used a kitchen knife for years without any lessons. They can cut vegetables, but they have never been shown how to hold a knife or the food, which knife suits which job, or how to look after a knife.

objectives.text: Hold a knife and the food safely: the pinch grip on the blade and the claw grip on the food.
Choose the right knife and cut for a job: chef's, paring or serrated knife, and slice, dice or julienne.
Keep a knife sharp and store it safely: honing, sharpening, washing and storing.

facts.text: In the claw grip the fingertips of the hand holding the food are curled back, and the knuckles guide the side of the blade.
A chef's knife is the all-round knife for most chopping and slicing on a board.
A paring knife is small and suits work done in the hand or on small items, such as peeling and trimming.
A serrated knife saws through bread and soft-skinned food such as tomatoes, because its teeth grip the surface where a smooth edge would slip.
A dice is a small cube, a julienne is a thin matchstick, and a slice is a flat cut across the food.
Honing straightens the edge of a knife that has bent a little with use; sharpening grinds away metal to make a new edge.
A knife should be washed by hand, dried, and stored in a block, sheath or magnetic strip, with its edge protected.

misconceptions.text: A dull knife is safer because it cuts less easily.
misconceptions.correction: A dull knife needs more force and slips off the food, so it is more dangerous; a sharp knife bites in and goes where you steer it.
Honing only straightens a bent edge; when a knife is truly dull it has to be sharpened, which removes metal.
